scenes.text: Our syllabus excerpt is conservation of energy. We will use the work energy principle, and see when mechanical energy is conserved. By the end, you can build a signed energy balance. Use it to find a resistance. And explain when mechanical energy is conserved.

scenes.title: A car coasts downhill

beats.text: Consider a car already moving down a straight hill. The driver lets it coast, with no driving force from the engine. Watch it travel towards the marked lower point, gaining speed as it descends.
Here is a snapshot as it passes the lower point. The car is still moving. Resistance has opposed the motion throughout; nevertheless, the car has gained speed.
We will use its energy change to find that resistance. First, the whole question.

scenes.title: The complete question

beats.text: A car of mass eight hundred kilograms coasts from A to B.
It travels one hundred metres along a straight slope, inclined at thirty degrees to the horizontal.
Its speed at A is ten metres per second.
Its speed at B is twenty metres per second.
There is no driving force. A constant resistance, F, acts uphill, opposite the motion. Model the car as a particle.
Take g as ten metres per second squared. Choose the lower point B as the zero height datum.
Use energy to find F. All the givens are now on the diagram. Pause and read them before we begin.

scenes.title: Vertical height and potential energy

beats.text: We need vertical height for gravitational potential energy. The road distance is the hypotenuse of this triangle; the height drop is opposite the slope angle.
So the vertical height equals distance along the slope times sine of the angle.
Substitute one hundred metres and thirty degrees.
This gives fifty metres. Put that height on the diagram.
Gravitational potential energy equals mass times g times height above our datum.
At A, substitute eight hundred, ten, and fifty.
The initial gravitational potential energy is four hundred thousand joules.
At B, height is zero. Mass times g times zero gives zero gravitational potential energy. This depends on our chosen datum.

scenes.title: Kinetic energy at both endpoints

beats.text: Now calculate the energy associated with motion. Kinetic energy equals one half mass times speed squared.
At A, the mass is eight hundred kilograms and the speed is ten metres per second. Square the speed first.
The initial kinetic energy is forty thousand joules.
At B, the same mass is moving at twenty metres per second.
The final kinetic energy is one hundred and sixty thousand joules.

The car has gained kinetic energy while losing gravitational potential energy. But resistance also transfers energy away. We must account for both effects, rather than equating the two energy changes.

scenes.title: Build the energy balance

beats.text: Write the general principle first. Initial mechanical energy plus signed work by non gravitational forces equals final mechanical energy.
Here E means kinetic plus gravitational potential energy. W excludes gravity, because gravity is already accounted for by the potential energy.
There is no driving work. Resistance is opposite the motion, so its work is negative F times distance along the road. The stationary road reaction is perpendicular to motion and does no work.
Therefore initial kinetic energy plus initial potential energy, minus F d, equals final kinetic energy plus final potential energy.
Substitute forty thousand, four hundred thousand, the road distance of one hundred, final kinetic energy of one hundred and sixty thousand, and zero final potential energy.
Combine the initial energies, then rearrange: one hundred F equals four hundred and forty thousand minus one hundred and sixty thousand.
Divide by one hundred. The resistance is two thousand eight hundred newtons, acting uphill.
These bars now show the calculated amounts on one scale. Initially there are four hundred and forty thousand joules. Finally, one hundred and sixty thousand remain as mechanical energy.
The difference is transferred to other forms, such as thermal energy. Energy has not been destroyed. The bars account for the same total.
beats.caption: Energy transferred, never destroyed

scenes.title: When is mechanical energy conserved?
scenes.source: Recording42–96 curved-track context; explicit PDF15–16 conservation bridge

beats.text: What would change with no resistance and no driving force? Consider a particle sliding on a smooth, stationary curved track.
The normal reaction is perpendicular to its motion at each point, so it does no work. Thus the total work by non gravitational forces is zero.
Use the same energy principle: initial energy plus that work equals final energy.
With zero work, initial kinetic plus potential energy equals final kinetic plus potential energy. Mechanical energy is conserved.
The track can curve. Potential energy depends on endpoint heights, not the length or shape of the route. On descending, potential energy decreases as kinetic energy increases.
Return to our resisting car. Is its mechanical energy conserved merely because there is no engine driving force? Think about the resistance.
beats.caption: No engine: is mechanical energy conserved?

beats.text: No. Resistance does negative work, transferring mechanical energy to other forms. No driving force alone is not enough.
beats.caption: Resistance transfers mechanical energy away

scenes.title: What you can now do

beats.text: You can build a signed energy balance: account for gravity once, through potential energy.
beats.caption: Build a signed energy balance

beats.text: Find a resistance using energy: road distance for its work, vertical height for potential energy.
beats.caption: Find a resistance using energy

beats.text: And explain when mechanical energy is conserved: zero total work by non gravitational forces.
beats.caption: Explain when mechanical energy is conserved
